tools.what_it_does: ISC-licensed community fork of Feather (24px grid, 2px stroke, ~1600-1900 icons); SVG files plus React/Vue/Svelte packages.

recommended_for.claim: Active Feather fork that keeps Feather's look and design guidelines but has many more icons
A good free stand-in for SF Symbols / Font Awesome on the web; works well with Svelte
Easy to vendor: copy only the few SVGs you use (attribution kept) rather than adding a dependency
Cleaner cross-platform than emoji for UI glyphs
Used as the icon set on landing pages and in production stacks

criticisms.claim: It is what LLM tools reach for by default (shadcn + Tailwind + lucide-react), so it now reads as a sign of an AI-generated, 'slop' site
Not distinctive: Lucide plus neutral Tailwind is 'unopinionated', the default when design was an afterthought, and people are tired of seeing static Lucide everywhere
Its license notice has to travel with the icon, which makes Lucide icons a poor base for a logo
Loading it per icon from an ESM CDN is fragile: ad blockers kill some icon files (e.g. 'fingerprint')

tools.strongest_criticism: Lucide is now an instant 'slop' tell because every LLM uses it unless told otherwise, so picking it hurts a brand that wants to look distinctive (46674925, 46667103).

tools.what_it_does: MIT-licensed SVG set from the Tailwind team (outline/solid/mini/micro); copy SVG/JSX from the site or use React/Vue packages.

recommended_for.claim: Tiny, elegant SVGs; a go-to set
The 'copy SVG/JSX' button makes it easy to paste inline SVG without adding a library
More consistent than Font Awesome; switching from FA to Heroicons improved alignment and screen-reader labelling
Works best inside the Tailwind/Headless UI ecosystem

criticisms.claim: The set is too small, so you end up adding Font Awesome or another set
Its MIT license confuses users about where the notice must go on a website

tools.strongest_criticism: Too small a set, so in practice you keep reaching for Font Awesome to fill gaps, which breaks visual consistency (29872253).

tools.what_it_does: MIT-licensed family of ~1,500 icons in six weights (thin/light/regular/bold/fill/duotone) on one grid; SVG, web components, React/Vue, Figma.

recommended_for.claim: Repeatedly named as a favourite / 'hidden gem'; stylish
Website shows off how flexibly the icons can be styled, and the docs are excellent
Roomy grid on its site (7 per row) makes the icons easy to scan
Used for logo-maker and product work, sourced via icones/Iconify

criticisms.claim: Still has gaps (e.g. no checked-bell); people turn to other sets or AI generation to fill missing glyphs

tools.strongest_criticism: Even a go-to set like Phosphor sometimes lacks the exact glyph needed, so people end up generating style-matched extras (45091117).

tools.what_it_does: Original MIT 24px/2px-stroke minimalist set (~287 icons); now largely superseded by Lucide.

recommended_for.claim: Clean, good design guidelines; a nice open-source set

criticisms.claim: Far too few icons; unmaintained relative to forks

tools.strongest_criticism: Feather is great but 'needs way way more icons', which is why people moved to Lucide (33225949).

tools.what_it_does: MIT 24px/2px-stroke set in the Feather style, ~4,500-5,900 icons; SVG, webfont and framework packages.

recommended_for.claim: Very large free set with design specs similar to Feather, so it suits anyone who wants the Feather/Lucide look plus coverage

criticisms.claim: The 'pixel perfect' claim is doubted; off-by-one pixel misalignment is common across sets
No easy way to keep Tabler/Lucide icons consistent between a web app and native toolchains

tools.strongest_criticism: Its 'pixel perfect' claim is doubted, since icon sets are 'still a Wild West' of off-by-one alignment errors (31122886).

tools.what_it_does: Aggregator of 200+ open-source sets (~200k-300k icons) with one naming scheme; HTTP API returning SVG, framework components, Figma plugin, used by icones.js.org and unplugin-icons.

recommended_for.claim: The single source for SVG icons; 'solved icons for us', and you can send a designer there to browse
Figma plugin used daily, so designers can drop the same icons into design files
Its API serves any icon as an SVG URL, handy for diagrams and templates
With unplugin-icons it ends the 'spaghetti' of icon setups: build-time import of only the icons you use
Covers brand logos too (Simple Icons is an Iconify pack), so separate logo sites aren't needed
Iconify plus some basic composition beats commissioning cheap Fiverr icons

criticisms.claim: Sites rebuilt on top of Iconify can drop each icon's license and attribution data (e.g. CC BY-SA sets)
Mixing sets from the catalog gives inconsistent sizes, so stick to one pack or expect to edit the SVGs
With so many sets it gets overwhelming, and there's no quick visual comparison

tools.strongest_criticism: Because it merges sets under different licenses, downstream tools can strip attribution: one clone omitted the CC BY-SA author and license info (34955665).

tools.what_it_does: Build-time plugin (Vite/webpack) that imports Iconify icons on demand as components.

recommended_for.claim: Paired with Iconify, it fixes messy icon setups

tools.strongest_criticism: No criticism found; only one comment mentions it (41600241).

tools.what_it_does: Google's huge set (variable font + SVG; outlined/rounded/sharp, fill/weight/grade axes), Apache 2.0.

recommended_for.claim: Huge coverage and a neutral style; a default unless a specific style is needed
Simple enough that you can draw your own icons that fit in
The rounded, outline or two-tone variants look less obviously Google
Used in place of the USWDS icons, which are roughly based on Material

criticisms.claim: Instantly looks/feels Google-related, which works against differentiation
The ligature icon font shows raw icon names as text when the font is blocked or fails

tools.strongest_criticism: Material instantly reads as 'something Google-related', so it is the wrong pick if you want to stand apart (46666306).

tools.what_it_does: Long-running icon set, once the default icon font, now SVG+JS/kits; free tier plus paid Pro with tens of thousands of icons.

recommended_for.claim: Free, covers the basics, and very easy to use
FA5+ is SVG-based, so you can import just the handful of icons you need
Better to build on a well-known set and add custom icons only where it matters
FA ligatures were meant to make the icons usable in design apps like InDesign

criticisms.claim: As an icon font it breaks when users disable custom fonts, and private-use glyphs are unreadable to screen readers
Alignment problems: only pixel-perfect at multiples of 14px; viewBox/margin inconsistencies need CSS hacks
Font Awesome itself recommends SVG over its webfont
It commoditized icons, so using it gives you a generic look

tools.strongest_criticism: Even FA has inconsistent SVG viewBox/size metrics, so icons sit misaligned next to each other unless you hard-code margins (35710469).

tools.what_it_does: Web app to cherry-pick icons from many sets plus your own SVGs and export a custom icon font or SVG sprite.

recommended_for.claim: Build a font/sprite with only the icons you need, including your own custom SVGs
Easiest and most flexible of the icon-compilation apps

criticisms.claim: Doesn't produce Compass markup for cross-browser support (minor gripe from 2014)

tools.strongest_criticism: No real criticism; the only complaint was missing Compass output (7345237).

tools.what_it_does: Huge crowd-sourced icon marketplace (CC BY / royalty-free / paid); also makes the Lingo brand-asset manager.

recommended_for.claim: Huge source with mixed CC BY and paid icons

criticisms.claim: Free SVGs come with junk you must clean out by hand unless you pay

tools.strongest_criticism: Unless you pay, you have to manually strip junk from the SVGs to make them usable (46670033).

tools.what_it_does: Commercial icon library (multiple styles/sizes, vector formats).

recommended_for.claim: Commercial-grade: two sizes, filled vs outline versions designed separately, free updates

criticisms.claim: Restrictive license (max 100 icons per project, per-project terms)

tools.strongest_criticism: Its 2014 license capped use at 100 icons per project, an odd and hard-to-enforce restriction (7345803).

tools.what_it_does: Commercial 2014 'icon system' (SVG with JS-driven size-specific detail, multicolour, states) plus free Open Iconic.

recommended_for.claim: Size-dependent detail, multicolour icons themable with a few CSS lines, available as SVG/webfont/PNG
Easy to implement on a personal site

criticisms.claim: Needs JavaScript to render the icons; not open source
Detail and weight vary between icons so they look like several sets shuffled; auto-swapping detail by size hurts consistency
Per-project paid licensing is too restrictive for teams

tools.strongest_criticism: Weight and detail vary so much that it looks like 'two or three different icon sets shuffled around', and size-swapping makes the same icon look different (7345682).

tools.what_it_does: Microsoft's MIT-licensed monochrome set (regular/filled, multiple sizes) for cross-platform apps.

recommended_for.claim: Pleasant, approachable, multi-platform, MIT
Monochrome SVGs can be recoloured with CSS and theme colours
Pared back on purpose, so it's a good base a design system can build on without too much personality

criticisms.claim: Bland monochrome icons that all look alike are bad for recognition
Couldn't set fill colours freely at launch; no Windows platform support

tools.strongest_criticism: Monochrome, look-alike icons 'are bad for users because they all look the same and lack color' (24992853).

recommended_for.claim: More detailed at large sizes; pairs with Font Awesome

criticisms.claim: The extra detail looks ugly at small sizes

tools.strongest_criticism: Ionicons' extra detail makes them ugly at small sizes (7345010).

recommended_for.claim: Another good open-source set

tools.what_it_does: Monochrome SVG brand logos (social/company), available on Iconify.

recommended_for.claim: Monochrome brand logos, with brand-guideline and license metadata to stay compliant

criticisms.claim: Companies' brand guidelines often require their official logo assets, so lookalike logo sets can break the rules

tools.strongest_criticism: Real brands often require their official logo files unaltered, so a lookalike logo set may break their guidelines (5546824).

tools.what_it_does: Search site for free SVGs with in-browser stroke/colour customization.

recommended_for.claim: Lets you adjust stroke width and colour and copy the edited SVG

criticisms.claim: No link to source/license; listed licenses are sometimes wrong

tools.strongest_criticism: License labels are sometimes wrong (e.g. CC artwork listed as MIT) and sources aren't linked (46666820).

approaches.pattern: Icon fonts (Font Awesome webfont, Material ligature font, IcoMoon fonts)

evidence.claim: Once won on IE support, single download, CSS colouring, and needing less CSS than sprite positioning
Breaks when users or the Tor browser block custom fonts, showing tofu or raw ligature names; fonts are an attack surface
Inaccessible: private-use glyphs and <i> tags give screen readers nothing
Can't tree-shake; subsetting needs special tools; harder to align
Once IE supported SVG there was no reason left for icon fonts; even Font Awesome now recommends SVG
Counterpoint: a font is fine for many icons, SVG for a few, so measure for your case

approaches.pattern: SVG sprite (<symbol> + <use href>) recoloured with currentColor

evidence.claim: One cached file; <svg><use href='sprite.svg#icon'/></svg> plus fill:currentColor inherits the text colour; wrap it in an icon component
Inlining the sprite in the HTML makes icons available before the JS bundle runs
Compile only the icons you need into one sprite to stay small (vs a 42KB Material font)
Gotchas: can't reference a symbol from a CSS background url; cross-browser trouble in XSLT; old browsers rasterised sprites badly; don't wrap bitmaps in SVG

approaches.pattern: Copy-paste / vendor raw inline SVGs (no icon library)

evidence.claim: Copy SVG/JSX buttons make it easy to paste only what you need
Vendoring a handful of Lucide SVGs (with attribution) instead of a dependency was praised
Inline SVG called the most capable and compatible 'gold standard'; Font Awesome's own site uses inline SVG
Inlining avoids layout shift, but it grows the DOM and can't be cached, so reserve width/height instead

approaches.pattern: Icons as framework components / npm packages

evidence.claim: Components give clear props, built-in accessibility and per-icon imports
Libraries often bundle the whole collection, inflating builds; viewBox/size inconsistencies remain
Per-icon ESM CDN loading is brittle (ad blockers, CDN mismatches)
An abandoned React wrapper forced a switch (Tabler UI)
SVGs from different libraries (and even one library) have subtly wrong viewBox/width/height, so they misalign side by side
Stick to one pack for size consistency, or be ready to edit SVGs
Varying detail and weight makes a set look like several sets shuffled together
People still mix sets to fill gaps (Font Awesome + Ionicons, Heroicons + Font Awesome)

approaches.pattern: Strict grid/stroke spec; extending a base set with custom icons drawn to its rules

evidence.claim: Treat icons as a system: encode grid, optical padding, stroke width, cap/join and corner radius, or stroke widths drift
Material is simple enough to draw your own matching icons; a neutral base set is a good starting point to build out
IcoMoon lets you add your own SVGs when the bought set lacks an icon
Build on a well-known set and add custom icons only where it matters
AI tools now restyle or generate icons to match a set's style (SF Symbols, Material, Phosphor, Lucide)
Rotted: domain-specific icons never get drawn, and a generic placeholder stays forever
LLMs drawing icons by hand get them wrong (a refresh arrow pointing the wrong way)

approaches.pattern: Monochrome, recolourable icons tinted by theme vs multicolour icons

evidence.claim: Monochrome lets the system apply 1-2 semantic/theme colours; avoids shipping light/dark/state variants
Multicolour icons themable via CSS were Iconic's selling point
Monochrome look-alikes hurt recognition (GIMP users switched colour icons back on)

approaches.pattern: License compliance and attribution for 'free' icons

evidence.claim: MIT/ISC sets need the notice kept; the usual advice is a /license or credits page, or a link inside the SVG
Using a licensed open-source icon as a logo means shipping its notice, which is awkward for branding
Aggregators and SEO sites mislabel or drop licenses (CC BY-SA, CC 4.0)
Commercial licenses capped per project or per icon count
Using a brand's logo usually means following its official brand guidelines

approaches.pattern: Size-specific icon detail (different drawings at small vs large sizes)

evidence.claim: Fewer details at small sizes improves legibility; few sets do it
Changing the drawing by size hurts consistency and recall
Hinting matters: SVG can't be hinted, while fonts can be grid-fitted

approaches.pattern: Animated icons (Lottie, JS motion libs, CSS-only SVG transitions)

evidence.claim: Animated Lucide ports are popular, but many animations are just stroke-draws or wiggles that don't convey meaning
Users asked for no-JS CSS/SVG hover versions; transform/opacity/stroke-draw can be flattened, springs and morphs can't
Lottie icons from designers mean a heavy JS player and a JSON format that devs find painful

approaches.pattern: Defaulting to the AI/shadcn stack icon set (Lucide)

evidence.claim: Lucide plus Inter plus all-caps badges now reads as an AI-made product
LLM system prompts hard-code lucide-react, which is why it is everywhere

articles_fetched.summary: Iconify is an open-source framework unifying many icon sets, now 300k+ vector icons, with developer libraries and an API. Iconify's code is MIT/Apache, but each icon set keeps its own license, so you have to check each set's terms.

Chris Coyier argues inline SVG via <symbol> sprites and <use> beats icon fonts: icons can be styled part by part with CSS, render more reliably and are semantically images (<title> works like alt text). Technique: combine the SVG files into one sprite (e.g. grunt-svgstore), include it at the top of the document, reference each icon with <use> and size it via CSS.

Lucide is ISC-licensed; icons derived from Feather also carry Cole Bemis's MIT notice. Both require the copyright/permission notice to be kept in copies, which is the attribution obligation HN commenters flagged for logos.
